subject: biology
title: Core practicals: biochemistry and enzymes
key_idea: An enzyme reaction is followed by measuring a product forming or a substrate disappearing over time. The initial rate is the fairest comparison. Temperature, pH and concentrations must be controlled. Colorimeters give numerical readings of colour change.

sections.heading: Measuring the progress of an enzyme-catalysed reaction

blocks.text: To investigate an enzyme, you follow how fast its substrate is used up or how fast its product forms. The rate is what you compare.

items: Measure the **rate of formation of a product**, for example the volume of oxygen collected from catalase breaking down hydrogen peroxide.
Measure the **rate of disappearance of a substrate**, for example the time for amylase to break down all the starch.
Measure at regular time intervals, so that you can draw a graph of amount against time.
Any other measure that changes as the reaction proceeds also works, such as a colour change or a pH change.

diagram.alt: Product formed against time: steepest at the start, then levelling off.

items: The **initial rate** is the rate at the very start, when the substrate concentration is highest and little product has built up.
Find it as the gradient of a tangent drawn to the curve at time zero.
Using initial rates gives a fair comparison, because the substrate has not yet run low and product is not slowing the reaction.

blocks.label: Rate of reaction
blocks.formula: rate = amount of product formed (or substrate used) ÷ time
where: amount = the volume, mass or concentration, with its unit
time = the time taken, in s

items: Rate is the change in product or substrate per unit time.
The initial rate is the gradient of the curve at the start.

sections.heading: Setting up a fair test with enzymes

blocks.text: Enzymes are sensitive to conditions, so everything except the independent variable must be controlled.

items: Keep temperature steady with a water bath, and let the solutions reach that temperature before mixing.
Use a buffer to hold pH constant.
Keep the volume and concentration of the enzyme and substrate the same, except for the variable being tested.
Start timing the instant the enzyme and substrate are mixed.
Repeat and calculate a mean for each condition.
To test enzyme concentration, make dilutions of the enzyme and keep the substrate the same.
To test substrate concentration, make dilutions of the substrate and keep the enzyme the same.
Plot rate against concentration. The rate rises, then levels off when another factor is limiting.
Control temperature, pH and the other concentrations.
Mix, then time straight away.

checks.q: Describe how you could find the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction from a graph of product against time.
checks.a: Draw a tangent to the curve at time zero (the start); calculate its gradient (change in product ÷ change in time).

checks.q: Give two reasons why the initial rate is used to compare enzyme activity under different conditions.
checks.a: Substrate concentration is at its highest and has not yet fallen; little product has built up; the enzyme has not begun to denature or be affected by conditions changing during the reaction.

checks.q: A student measures the rate of an enzyme at several temperatures. State three variables to control.
checks.a: Any three from: pH (buffer); enzyme concentration; substrate concentration; volume of enzyme and substrate; time before measurement starts.

blocks.text: Core practical: vitamin C content of food and drink
Vitamin C reduces the blue dye DCPIP to colourless. The more vitamin C a sample has, the less of it is needed to decolourise the dye.

items.text: Add solutions of known vitamin C concentration, drop by drop, to a fixed volume of DCPIP and record the volume needed to decolourise it.
Plot a calibration graph of volume used against vitamin C concentration.
Repeat with the food or drink, and read the concentration from the graph.
Repeat each test and calculate a mean.

items: Control the volume and concentration of DCPIP, and the temperature.
Add the juice slowly with a pipette or burette and swirl, so the end point is clear.
A coloured juice makes the end point hard to see. Dilute it or compare against a colour standard.

blocks.text: Core practical: enzyme and substrate concentrations

items: Vary the concentration of the enzyme with the substrate in excess, or vary the substrate with the enzyme held constant.
Measure the initial rate of reaction at each concentration, and plot it against concentration.
At low concentration the rate is proportional to concentration. At higher concentration it levels off, as another factor limits the rate.
Run the reaction at a range of temperatures in water baths. Measure the initial rate at each.
The rate rises to an optimum, then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures.
The **temperature coefficient, Q₁₀**, shows how much the rate changes for a 10 °C rise.

blocks.label: Temperature coefficient
blocks.formula: Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10) °C ÷ rate at T °C
where: rate = the rate of reaction at each temperature, in the same unit

blocks.text: A Q₁₀ of 2 means the rate doubles for each 10 °C rise. For two temperatures not 10 °C apart, use the equation below.

blocks.label: Q₁₀ for any two temperatures
where: R₁, R₂ = the rates at T₁ and T₂
T₁, T₂ = the two temperatures, in °C, with T₂ greater than T₁

diagram.alt: A Q10 calculation with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: An enzyme reaction has a rate of {r1} units at 20 °C and {r2} units at 30 °C. Calculate Q₁₀.
working: The temperatures are 10 °C apart, so Q₁₀ = rate at 30 °C ÷ rate at 20 °C.

items: DCPIP decolourises as vitamin C is added.
Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10) ÷ rate at T; use it only below the optimum.

blocks.text: Catalase: rate of formation of a product

items: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen.
Collect the oxygen over water or in a gas syringe, and record the volume at regular time intervals.
Plot volume against time. The initial rate is the gradient at the start.
Tissue such as liver or potato is a source of catalase. Use equal masses of the same size pieces.

blocks.text: Amylase: rate of disappearance of a substrate

items: Amylase breaks down starch to maltose.
Add samples of the mixture at regular intervals to iodine solution on a spotting tile.
The iodine stays blue-black while starch remains and stays orange-brown when all the starch has gone.
The time taken for the blue-black colour to disappear shows the rate: the shorter the time, the faster the rate.
A colorimeter measures how much light passes through a coloured solution, in absorbance or transmission.
It follows a reaction with a colour change, such as starch with iodine as it is broken down.
Zero it with a blank, choose a filter of a complementary colour and take readings at set times.
It gives numerical data and avoids judging a colour by eye, so it is more objective.
Catalase: measure product; amylase: measure substrate.
A colorimeter replaces judging a colour by eye with a numerical reading.
